newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Insurance brokers want EU passport.
newsitem.headline: Insurance brokers want EU passport.

text.p: Insurance agents and brokers urged the European Commission on Monday to abolish national obstacles to the profession saying they were not getting their fair share of the EU's single market.
Self-employed insurance intermediaries account for the vast majority of insurance products sold in Europe.
But to get the so-called single passport to operate throughout the 15-nation bloc they have to comply with a vast array of complex and lengthy national rules.

The EU's insurance market was completely liberalised in July 1996. But that only applies to insurance firms which no longer need to create subsidiaries or seek authorisations to operate outside their home market.

Independent insurance intermediaries are not covered despite having about 80 percent of the overall insurance market in Germany, 75 percent in Belgium and 69 percent in Britain, according to the International Federation of Insurance Intermediaries (BIPAR).
BIPAR and the European Consumers' Organisation (BEUC) called in a joint statement for binding legislation to ensure a truly European market for insurance professionals.

"(...) BEUC and BIPAR are warning that failure by the Commission to take rapidly the necessary action in this area will mean that the single market in insurance will continue to remain an illusion both for consumers and for the industry," the statement said.
Legally speaking, nothing prevents say a French or Dutch broker from operating in Belgium -- nothing, that is but highly dissuasive rules.

"He must first register and for that he needs to meet different conditions including that the products he'll be offering comply with Belgian 'general interest' rules," BIPAR's legal adviser, Isabelle Audigier, told Reuters.
"This is a very difficult, long and expensive process," Audigier added.
Belgium is by no means alone in making life difficult for foreign brokers.
What general interest rules mean to the insurance sector nobody knows exactly, but they are usually seen as an excuse to to protect national markets from foreign competition.
The EU adopted measures in 1976 designed to help insurance agents and brokers to establish themselves and provide services in the EU market of their choice.
But the 20-year-old legislation, backed by more recent non-binding rules, failed to bring down national barriers, the joint statement said.
The Commission is expected to put forward new legislation.
